rule: Every number on screen or in VO must be listed here with a source URL. `display` is the exact on-screen string. `confidence`: verified = read in the primary source; secondary = reputable secondary source; anecdote = widely reported story, label it on screen.

facts.claim: Williams-Sonoma sold a bread maker at $275 that sold poorly; after adding a larger model at $429 (roughly 1.5x the price), sales of the $275 model roughly doubled.
facts.sourceTitle: Simonson & Tversky (1992), 'Choice in Context: Tradeoff Contrast and Extremeness Aversion', Journal of Marketing Research 29(3) — the compromise/decoy effect; the Williams-Sonoma bread-maker story is the standard illustration (also told in Ariely, 'Predictably Irrational', 2008, and in HBR).
facts.quote: Widely reported anecdote; exact sales figures were never published, 'nearly doubled' is how the story is told.
facts.note: VO says 'almost twice the price' for $275 → $429 (1.56×). Acceptable as spoken rounding; do not display '2× the price'.

facts.claim: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) spun a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at 10 or 65, then asked subjects the percentage of African countries in the UN. Median estimates were 25 (wheel = 10) and 45 (wheel = 65).
facts.sourceTitle: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
facts.quote: The median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations were 25 and 45 for groups that received 10 and 65, respectively, as starting points.

facts.claim: Illustrative everyday anchors: a $90 steak on a menu, a tag reading 'was $199 / now $129'.
facts.note: Not presented as measurements; no source line needed, but never present them as 'a study found'.
